intended_object: An integral lattice (L, b) is negative definite when b(x, x) < 0 for every nonzero x. Equivalently, the quadratic form −q is positive definite. This comes from the docstring and the module doc, which cites Ebeling, Lattices and Codes, Ch. 1.
explanation:
An `IntegralLattice V` consists of a full ℤ-lattice in the ℚ-vector space V together with a symmetric rational bilinear form on V. The definition asks that the negation of the associated quadratic map is `QuadraticMap.PosDef`. Unfolded, that means −b(x, x) > 0, i.e. b(x, x) < 0, for every nonzero x ∈ V.

The condition is stated on all of V rather than only on lattice vectors. The two versions are equivalent, because the lattice spans V over ℚ (the `isLattice` field): every rational vector is a positive integer multiple of a lattice vector, and multiplying by that integer scales q(x) by a positive square.

This matches the standard notion, and it sits alongside the library's `IsPosDef`, which is the same predicate without the negation. Mathlib has no separate negative-definiteness predicate for quadratic maps (a grep for `NegDef` finds nothing). Mathlib does have `PosDef` for quadratic maps, and this definition simply applies it to −q. The setting is that of the library's integral lattices, which is the standard one, so the definition is not too narrow.
